en: XXX. The Chapter on the Instruction on the Characteristics of Forms such as the Variegated (*citrādi*) *Saṃvarodayatantra*, Chapter XXX, translated by Claudio Cicuzza, Rome.
Now I shall speak of another [method]; listen, O Lord of the Guhyakas.
The painted form of the deity possesses the characteristics of a majestic and imposing appearance. //30-1//
The seat (*āsana*) of the form of the Brahma-line and so forth consists of five parts;
it is divided into three sections for the limbs, with the face occupying equal portions. (30-2)
The face is twelve parts, the neck is four finger-breadths; its neck, throat, and so forth, as well as the two ears, should be well-proportioned with beautiful eyes. (30.3)
The face consists of three parts: the forehead, the mouth, and the nose;
the face including the eyebrows is two finger-breadths above [the nose], and the eyes are two finger-breadths [above that]. (30.4)
Even for that [body] cut into four-finger-width sections, when fully extended,
it reaches the middle of the neck from the point where the two beautiful parts have met at the center. //30-5//
Even in the region of the heart, [the breath] moves from the navel as one [unit] in every direction;
for that which has moved into the space between the breasts, it proceeds from both breasts, just as when it has moved into the chest. //30-6//
But when two [fingers] are grasped by the hand, it is called *krāntaka* because he has two in his hand;
it is provided with four fingers and endowed with thighs and shanks. (30.7)
The shoulder portion shall be four finger-breadths, and likewise it should extend down to the feet;
for one measuring twelve *tālas*, it is adorned with the forms of deities. (30.8)
When four finger-breadths remain, the seats are formed by the eight positions;
by means of the bound seats and non-seats, [the distance] increases by one finger-breadth at each step. //30-9//
One should fashion the intestines, the small intestines, and so forth, within the interior of a moon disc;
this is the profound Vajradeva, characterized by twelve tālas in height. //30-10//
The lower portion and other parts are adorned with various ornaments;
that [posture] is also characterized by the two arms being restrained while the tāla is stepped upon. (30-11)
One should worship the gentle deity Citra with two fingers;
he too, having made his mouth like a palm tree, shall always satisfy one from his belly. (30.12)
One should join every joint with every joint using two fingers;
[these are] Krodha, Krodheśvarī, the Goddess, Ceṭī, Ceṭī, and Kiṃkarī. //30-13//
The form that is terrible and loathsome, however, is adorned with ten *tālas*;
the form consisting of mind (*manomaya*), however, is adorned with nine *tālas*. //30-14//
The deities of the maṇḍala circle should be joined in successive order;
these [deities] are adorned with various characteristics in the center of the Vajrarāja. (30.15)

If the chin and neck are three times longer than they should be, or if the shanks are excessively long, it portends expulsion and loss of status for practitioners of mantra who are otherwise self-controlled. (30.16)
If the nose, ears, and other [limbs] are shorter than three finger-breadths,
there will certainly be a loss of accomplishment as well as a loss of prosperity. (30-17)

Practitioners of fixed resolve who possess the glory of overcoming Māra and obstacles remain far removed from the three great defects of the thighs and feet, and from swellings on the calves and so forth. (30.18)
If the skull, thighs, and cage-like frame of the body are sunken and greatly defective, there will be a swift loss of wealth; of this there is no doubt. //30-19//
If there are three marks on the forehead, the two ears, or the two breasts,
practitioners will very soon experience quarrels and affliction from enemies. (30-20)
Indeed, there are three great defects: thighs that are too large, a body that is too large, and a chest that is too broad;
furthermore, there is fear of thieves and of deaths—of this there is no doubt. (30.21)
For those self-controlled practitioners of mantra, there shall be squinting eyes, a broken nose, deformities of the ears, lips, and forehead, various obstacles, and even death. (30.22)
If the breath is directed upward and the posture is unstable due to shifting, there will be loss of wealth; indeed, one's own seat is always shaken when the posture wavers. (30-23)
The limbs beginning with the snake-neck (uragrīva) have been described as having innumerable defects;
they possess the signs and mudrās of the reversal of the mere [elements] beginning with the eye. (30.24)
The characteristic of the suffering of grief and torment consists of universal defects and so forth;
the defect of distress is characterized by the three [defenses]: reliance, the parasol, and the seat. (30.25)
Death occurs for one who has fallen from prosperity due to those who speak unpleasant and disagreeable words;
having observed this great defect among faults, one should be well-discerning. (30.26)
Trained in all arts, depicted with perfect composure, complete with all the auspicious marks, and possessing a beautiful form that delights the sight. (30.27)
The form was exceedingly gentle yet fierce and terrifying;
it possessed the pride of a heroic hero's body, while its face was graced with amorous smiles.
Thus, for practitioners of mantras who possess these characteristics, one should have a painted cloth [mandala] prepared;
for beginner practitioners of mantras, one should have a reflected image or similar representation made.
Success is swiftly attained; having spread out the cloth-painting, one should perform the practice. //30-29//
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the description of the characteristics of forms such as the variegated and so forth.
